title: OpenCLI generic extensions
description: The x-interactive, x-environment and x-passthrough extensions of an OpenCLI document. Validate a document against this schema AND the base OpenCLI schema: this one checks only these three keys (walking the command tree to find them) and leaves every other key to the base schema. Objects are open, like the base schema's.

x-passthrough.description: x-passthrough marks a command; the document root is not one.

Command.description: A command of the document, walked only to reach its extensions and its subcommands.

XInteractive.description: What a running interactive session accepts. The commands are typed inside the session, not on the command line: they are written without the prefix the session reads them with (`model`, not `/model`), and a docs site makes no page for them.

commands.description: The commands typed inside the session

keys.description: The key bindings of the session

InteractiveCommand.description: A command typed inside an interactive session. Its shape is the OpenCLI command's, without extensions of its own.

name.description: The command name, without the session's prefix

x-interactive.description: A session command does not open another session.

x-passthrough.description: A session command is not run by the host program.

Named.description: An argument or an option of a session command.

KeyBinding.description: One key binding of an interactive session.

keys.description: The keys that trigger it (`ctrl+c`, `esc`), any one of them

context.description: Where the binding applies, when not everywhere (a picker, the composer)

XEnvironment.description: The environment variables the command reads.

values.description: The values it accepts, when it is not free-form

XPassthrough.description: The host hands every argument after this command, unparsed, to another program, except two it reads first: its own recursive options given right after the command (before the first argument of the program), which the host parses, and a `--` right after the command or after those options, which only ends them and is not handed on. From the first other argument on, everything is the program's, `--help` and a later `--` included. The command's arguments, options and subcommands, if any, document that program; code generators never read them.

program.description: The program the arguments are handed to, when it is not named like the command
